content:
Sets looks like the softest chapter in JEE Maths. That is the trap. Setters hide two-set and three-set counting that eats marks fast. So take the free JEE Sets Relations and Functions online test below. It has 15 exam MCQs and scores you at once. Each answer gives a short reason. Aim for 12 out of 15.

What JEE asks from this chapter

The paper mixes theory with counting. First come set laws and Venn regions. Then relations turn up. Functions close it with domain and range.

  • Union, intersection and the rest of the set laws.
  • Two-set and three-set counting with the overlap rule.
  • Checks that make a relation reflexive or symmetric.
  • Relations that split a set into classes.
  • Domain, range and the kind of a function.

Formulas and facts to revise first

  • Count a union as n(A) plus n(B) minus the overlap.
  • That way you never double count the shared part.
  • A set with n parts has two to the power n subsets.
  • A relation is an equivalence only if all three checks pass.
  • The range of a sin x stays between minus a and a.

Mistakes that cost JEE marks

  • Adding n(A) and n(B) but not taking off the overlap.
  • Calling a relation symmetric after just one pair.
  • Mixing up A minus B with B minus A in a gap.
  • Marking a set non-empty when no value fits it.

quiz.intro: Fifteen exam-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Let A, B and C be subsets of a universal set with A ∩ B = A ∩ C and A ∪ B = A ∪ C. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: Both conditions force B and C to share the same elements. When intersections with A and unions with A agree, B must equal C.

questions.q: The set A = { x : x is rational and x² = 2 } is a:
questions.explanation: x² = 2 gives x = ±√2, and both are irrational. No rational number fits, so the set is empty.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram with three sets A, B and C, the region (A ∩ B ∩ C)′ is:
options: The intersection of A, B and C.
The complement of the universal set.
The whole universal set except the intersection of A, B and C.
The union of A, B and C.
questions.explanation: The complement of A ∩ B ∩ C holds every element outside that triple overlap. So it is the universal set minus the intersection.

questions.q: Two finite sets have m and n elements. The first has 56 more subsets than the second. Then m and n are:
questions.explanation: 2^m − 2^n = 56 factors as 2³(2³ − 1). Matching the parts gives n = 3 and m = 6.
Distribute to get A ∪ (B ∩ B′). Since B ∩ B′ is empty, the result is A.

questions.q: Which of these sets is finite?
options: x ∈ ℕ where x is even
questions.explanation: Only the integers from −5 to 5 form a finite list of 11 values. Each of the other three sets holds infinitely many numbers.

questions.q: Of 500 car owners in Delhi, 400 own car A, 200 own car B and 50 own both. Is the data correct?
options: Yes, assuming some own three cars.
questions.explanation: n(A ∪ B) = 400 + 200 − 50 = 550. That exceeds the 500 people surveyed, so the data cannot be right.

questions.q: For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, the symmetric difference A Δ B is:
questions.explanation: A Δ B keeps elements in exactly one set. Here A − B = {1} and B − A = {4}, so the answer is {1, 4}.
A′ = {4, 5, 6}. Its intersection with B = {3, 4} is just {4}.

questions.q: In an exam 60% passed Maths, 50% passed Physics and 20% passed both. What percentage failed both?
questions.explanation: Passed at least one = 60 + 50 − 20 = 90 percent. So the percentage failing both is 100 − 90 = 10 percent.
It has all three self-pairs, so it is reflexive. It lacks (2,1), so it is not symmetric, but no case breaks transitivity.

questions.q: R on the rationals is defined by a R b when a − b is an integer. This relation is:
questions.explanation: a − a = 0 is an integer, differences reverse in sign, and integer differences add. So R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

questions.q: The range of f(x) = 3 sin x is:
questions.explanation: The range of sin x is [−1, 1]. Multiplying by 3 stretches it to [−3, 3].

questions.q: For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {1, 2}, which is true?
options: B is a strict superset of A.
A is a strict superset of B.
questions.explanation: Every element of B lies in A, and A also holds 3. So A is a strict superset of B.
A ∩ B = {2, 3} and B ∩ C = {3}. Their union is {2, 3}.
